newsitem.title: INDIA: Housewife-turned-leader wins vote in India state.
newsitem.headline: Housewife-turned-leader wins vote in India state.

text.p: A quiet housewife who was made chief minister of India's second most populous state by her scandal-tainted husband won a confidence vote in the state assembly on Monday.

State officials said that Rabri Devi, who succeeded her husband Laloo Prasad Yadav in the eastern Bihar state, won 194 votes in favour and 110 against in a confidence vote in the 325-state legislative assembly at Patna, the state capital.
"You help me and I will help you," the 38-year-old mother of seven daughters and two sons told the assembly while seeking the vote that came after Friday's election.
The vote rattled India's ruling coalition and angered opposition groups.

Devi, who has not studied beyond primary school, was suddenly named successor by Yadav, a charismatic low-caste leader who resigned on Friday after a court issued a warrant for his arrest in a $280-million corruption scandal case.

India's Supreme Court stayed Yadav's arrest until its hearing was over on his appeal against detention sought by federal police. Yadav has been indicted in a case that involves alleged embezzlement of animal welfare funds.

"I will learn governance as I did cooking and milking cows," Rabri Devi said on Saturday a day after taking office to head the state of more than 86 million people, where 61 percent of the population is illiterate.
At a news conference, Devi blushed at each question and looked at her chaperoning husband before answering.
"Even if my husband is acquitted, I will remain chief minister," the Pioneer newspaper quoted her on Monday as saying. In a television interview, she gave monosyllabic answers.

Yadav, citing differences over internal elections, formed his Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) party last month after breaking from Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's Janata Dal party, which leads India's 15-party United Front (UF) government.

Devi received support on Monday from India's leading Congress party, which sees Yadav's group as a bulwark against rival Hindu nationalists, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), whom it accuses of a bias against Moslems.
The BJP slammed Gujral's coalition and the Congress, which closed ranks last year to oust a 12-day-old BJP government from power in a fragmented parliament.
"Nothing illustrates the utterly unscrupulous nature of the UF-Congress alliance better than yesterday's grotesque developments in Bihar," BJP president L.K. Advani said on Saturday.
Yadav's refusal to resign from office created a rift between hardliners and moderates in the United Front, which decided late on Friday not to admit his group in its fold.

The BJP's national executive slammed Gujral on Sunday for dragging his feet in seeking the removal of Yadav from office. "In a sense, it would be futile to expect this Prime Minister to act, to take a principled stand," it said in a resolution.
Gujral has faced much criticism in dealing with Yadav. The prime minister had for weeks asked Yadav to quit, but repeatedly said he had no legal authority to make him leave his chair.
